ux-day.body:
“Being you is the only differentiator.”

A day to remember at Microsoft.

In a world where tools are constantly changing, AI is evolving every single day, and everyone is trying to become more and more... maybe somewhere in between, we start losing ourselves.

But one thing that will stay with me from UX Day 2026 is this:
being you is the only differentiator.

Some experiences don’t just teach you skills, they quietly change the way you see yourself, your work, and the direction you want to move toward. This was one of those experiences for me.

Listening to the speakers made me realize something important:

We need to evolve.
We need to unlearn.
And then learn again.

In design, growth is not just about mastering tools or frameworks. It’s about changing the way we observe people, tell stories, express emotions, and create experiences that truly connect.

One of the most powerful things I heard was:
“Vulnerability is a design skill.”

Because great storytelling does not come from perfection.

It comes from honesty.

From empathy.

From being human enough to understand another human.

Every conversation, every session, every insight shared at the Microsoft office gave me a new perspective and a new direction to move forward with. I walked in hoping to learn more about UX, but I walked out thinking more deeply about people, emotions, storytelling, and the kind of designer I want to become.

Grateful for the speakers, the conversations, the energy in the room, and the reminder that design is not just about solving problems.
It’s about understanding people first.

config.body:
Attended Config Friends of Figma, Jaipur on 27th June, and it was an insightful experience with valuable perspectives on design, AI integration, and building products that create real impact.

One idea that really stayed with me was: People don't buy interfaces, they buy outcomes.

As someone who's often found myself thinking beyond just screens and interactions, this resonated deeply. I've always believed that great design isn't only about creating beautiful experiences. It's about understanding the business, solving the right problems, and creating meaningful impact.
Grateful for the learning and looking forward to applying these insights in my design journey.

ai-designers.body:
“AI is replacing UI/UX designers.”

That’s what everyone’s saying lately.

But here’s the thing—AI might design a UI, but it can’t understand a human.
It can generate layouts, color palettes, or even full prototypes in seconds.
 
What it can’t do is empathize with a user who’s frustrated, confused, or inspired.

UX isn’t just about making screens look good.

It’s about understanding why people behave the way they do—and designing around that.

AI can assist in execution.

But the thinking, research, and emotion behind a great user experience still need a human mind.

So no, AI isn’t replacing UX designers.
It’s just raising the bar for who’s willing to think deeper. 💬

present-your-way.body:
So we were given a task to present our user testing research — everything from initial research to interviews to final insights.

But here’s the twist.

No traditional PPT.

No fixed format.

Just one instruction: present it your way.

What this really meant was... how creatively can you tell a story?

We ditched slides and built a Snake & Ladders experience.

Why?

Because our process wasn’t linear.

It looked exactly like that board.

Climbing up with insights.

Sliding down with failed assumptions.

Going back, rethinking, testing again.

Every ladder was a breakthrough.

Every snake was a reality check.

And suddenly, research stopped feeling like documentation...

It became a journey you could see, feel, and play.

And yes, we even got some really cool bookmarks for our idea and effort — small reward, big validation.

Welcome to a design classroom
where storytelling matters more than slides.

Built this with: Akanksha singh

system-1.body:
I recently started reading Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman

Most users don't make decisions logically.

They make them instinctively.

Kahneman calls this  System 1: fast, automatic, emotional thinking.

That's exactly what many successful products are designed for.

 • Instagram's infinite scroll removes stopping points.
 • Netflix autoplay keeps momentum.
 • Swiggy and Zomato lead with visuals, discounts, and delivery time before users compare options.
 • Apple sells the feeling first and the specifications later.

As designers, we often say we're reducing friction.

But what we're really reducing is the amount of System 2 thinking required.

Every extra click, every unnecessary form field, and every confusing navigation menu forces users to stop and think.

The best interfaces don't remove thinking altogether. 

They reserve deliberate thinking for decisions that actually matter.

That's a design principle I'm paying much more attention to now.

railways-2050.body:
What happens when you get 4.5 hours to redesign Indian Railways for 2050?

Today was intense.

We were given a live design sprint:
First, deeply analyze the mismatches in the current Indian Railways system. Not surface-level complaints. Real gaps between what the system demands and what users can actually do.

We mapped problems across accessibility — visual, motor, cognitive, situational, temporary.

From unclear coach positions to digital booking stress.
From overcrowded platforms to lack of assisted boarding.

Then came the real challenge:
Reimagine Indian Railways in 2050.

Not just an app redesign.
A complete ecosystem shift.

I designed:
 • Guided floor pathways
 • Assisted mobility e-carts
 • Simple e-coupon tickets instead of long PDFs
 • Ramp-based boarding
 • Secure luggage compartments
 • Women-reserved berths for safety

This sprint reminded me:

Accessibility is not a feature.
It’s dignity in motion.

And maybe the future of Indian Railways isn’t about making trains faster.
Maybe it’s about making journeys calmer.

Ps: Internet and AI were allowed (thankfully 😅)

braille.body:
I ran my fingers over a train seat number before I read it.

Not by accident.

Out of curiosity.

The numbers were embossed in Braille.

And for a second, I just paused.

Because that tiny detail wasn’t made for me.

Somewhere in the early 2000s, someone in Indian Railways decided:

“Navigation shouldn’t depend on sight alone.”

Just... a quiet layer of accessibility built into everyday travel.

Millions pass by it.

Few notice it.

But for someone, that detail changes everything.

Good systems don’t just serve the majority.

They acknowledge the edges.

Even when those edges are invisible to most.

That one detail taught me something:

User-centric design isn’t loud.
It’s thoughtful.
It shows up in places
where no one is clapping.

anchoring.body:
Today I learned how Anchoring Bias quietly influences our decisions in digital products.

I was about to watch a series on Sony LIV and landed on their subscription page. While looking at the plans, one thing immediately caught my attention: the highlighted ₹1499 yearly plan.

That's when I noticed Anchoring Bias in action.

The first number we see often becomes our reference point. Once my brain saw ₹1499, I automatically started comparing every other plan against it rather than evaluating each option independently.

The interesting part is that the highlighted plan doesn't just show a price—it shapes how the other prices are perceived.

It's fascinating how a few design decisions can influence choices without users even realizing it.

UX is not just about designing interfaces.

It's about understanding how people think and make decisions.

variable-rewards.body:
Today I was reading Atomic Habits and came across the concept of Variable rewards.

And suddenly, so many UI/UX decisions started making sense to me.

The idea is simple:

People feel more excited when they don’t know exactly what reward they’ll get.

That small element of surprise keeps curiosity alive.

And once you notice it, you’ll start seeing it everywhere in products.

Think about apps like BigBasket, Zomato, or Blinkit.

Sometimes you open the app and suddenly see:

“Flat ₹125 OFF”
“Free delivery today”
“Extra cashback unlocked”

You weren’t expecting it.

That tiny surprise creates excitement.

Because if users got the exact same reward every single time, eventually it would feel normal and predictable.

But variable rewards make users think:

“Maybe there’s something interesting today.”

And that curiosity is powerful.

What I found interesting is that this is not just psychology.

It’s also a product strategy.

A lot of great digital experiences are designed around keeping users emotionally engaged, not just functionally satisfied.

Now every time I open an app and see those random rewards or surprise offers, I look at it less like a discount...
...and more like a very intentional UX decision.

scarcity.body:
I recently visited an art exhibition and something clicked from a UX psychology lens: Induced scarcity. 

Induced scarcity isn’t about tricking people.
It’s about focus.

When something is limited, we don’t just want it more.
We pay attention differently.

That’s exactly what happens in a well-curated gallery.

Fewer artworks.
More space.
Longer pauses.

You slow down without realizing it.

You stand there a beat longer.

You remember what you saw.

And that’s the part most digital products miss.

We keep adding.

More features.
More sections.
More options.

Thinking abundance equals value.

But often, it does the opposite.

Good design doesn’t overwhelm.
It invites.

Just like a gallery that trusts one artwork to hold a room.

Different medium.
Same psychology.
